Find Valid Polynomial Pools Configurations

Source: R/pp_matrix.R
pp_design.Rd

Enumerate PP parameter combinations that satisfy user-supplied design constraints, so that candidate pooling matrices can be planned before calling pp_matrix.

Usage

pp_design(
  N_min = 50,
  N_max = 1000,
  M_max = 500,
  k_min = 2,
  pool_size_max = 500
)

Arguments

N_min

Integer scalar giving the minimum allowed number of individuals \(N\). Only PP configurations with \(q^d \ge N_{\min}\) are retained.

N_max

Integer scalar giving the maximum allowed number of individuals \(N\). Only PP configurations with \(q^d \le N_{\max}\) are retained.

M_max

Integer scalar giving the maximum allowed number of pools \(J\). The default is 500.

k_min

Integer scalar giving the minimum required COMP detection limit \(k_{\max} = \lfloor (n_l - 1)/(d - 1) \rfloor\). The default is 2.

pool_size_max

Integer scalar giving the maximum allowable canonical pool size \(q^{d-1}\). The default is 500.

Value

A data frame with one row per retained PP configuration and columns:

q

Integer; Galois Field order (prime power)

d

Integer; dimension

nl

Integer; number of layers

N

Integer; maximum samples (\(q^d\))

M

Integer; legacy display alias for the number of pools \(J = n_l q\)

pool_size

Integer; samples per pool (\(q^{d-1}\))

k_max

Integer; detection limit

compression

Numeric; display alias for the compression ratio \(N/J\)

The rows are sorted by decreasing compression and then by increasing pool_size. The function returns NULL if no configuration satisfies the supplied constraints.

Details

For each candidate PP parameter tuple \((q, d, n_l)\), the associated full design has $$N = q^d, \qquad J = n_l q, \qquad n_j = q^{d-1}, \qquad w_i = n_l.$$ The COMP exact-decoding guarantee for PP designs is governed by $$k_{\max} = \left\lfloor \frac{n_l - 1}{d - 1} \right\rfloor.$$ This function searches a finite library of supported prime powers \(q\) and dimensions \(d \in \{2,3,4\}\), filters the resulting tuples by the user constraints, and reports the compression factor $$\frac{N}{J}.$$ The output is intended for planning rather than for direct matrix generation; once a row is selected, pp_matrix can be used to construct the corresponding \(\mathbf{M} \in \{0,1\}^{J \times N}\).

Relationship to pp_matrix and pp_verify

  • pp_design: Finds valid parameter combinations (planning)

  • pp_matrix: Generates the actual pooling matrix (construction)

  • pp_verify: Checks properties of a generated matrix (validation)

Typical workflow:

# 1. Find suitable configurations
configs <- pp_design(N_min = 300, N_max = 500)

# 2. Choose one and generate matrix
M <- pp_matrix(q = 8, d = 3, nl = 6, N = 384)

# 3. Verify the matrix
pp_verify(M)

Generalization Rules

The PP algorithm generalizes to any \((q, d, n_l)\) where:

  1. \(q\) is a prime power: 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 16, 25, 27, ...

  2. \(d \geq 2\) (dimension)

  3. \(1 \leq n_l \leq q + 1\) (number of layers)

What You CANNOT Choose Arbitrarily

ConstraintWhy
\(q\) must be prime powerGalois Fields only exist for prime power orders
\(M = n_l \times q\)Each layer contributes exactly \(q\) pools
Pool size = \(q^{d-1}\)Fixed by the polynomial structure

Design Selection Guide

SamplesRecommendedPoolsCompression
~64q=4, d=3, nl=5203.2x
~384q=8, d=3, nl=6488x
~729q=9, d=3, nl=76311.6x
~4096q=16, d=3, nl=914428x

References

Tan, Y. H. I. (2020). Pooling matrix designs for group testing. SIAM Undergraduate Research Online, 13, 1-21.

Aldridge, M., Johnson, O., & Scarlett, J. (2019). Group testing: An information theory perspective. Foundations and Trends in Communications and Information Theory, 15(3-4), 196-392.

configs <- pp_design(N_min = 300, N_max = 500)
